hook_text: Every time a Mpumalanga power station fires up, it burns sunlight that fell before the dinosaurs.
clip_script: Three hundred million years ago, South Africa was swampy forest. Trees with tongue-shaped leaves soaked up sunlight and stored its energy. They died, fell into oxygen-poor water and did not rot. Layer on layer of peat. Then sand and mud buried it, and heat and crushing pressure cooked it, for millions of years, into coal. Now we dig it up and burn it, releasing that ancient sunshine to boil water and spin turbines. The catch? It took hundreds of millions of years to make, and we burn thousands of tonnes a day. Once it is gone, it is gone. That is non-renewable. The fresh sunshine landing on solar panels, though, arrives every single morning.
visual_style: Whiteboard timeline: a swamp forest, a layer of peat, rock layers piling on with pressure arrows, a coal seam, then a power station chimney; ending with a solar panel under a rising sun.
pacing: Grand opening, a fast time-lapse middle, a reflective close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and trace a lump of coal back to the swamp.
